title: Suraqa's horse
hook: Suraqa, chasing for the reward, sinks in the sand and turns back (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asma tore her waistband to tie the food bags. Your line was: two belts.

A price on two heads. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Suraqa ibn Malik tells this story himself. Messengers from Quraysh came to his tribe, offering a reward to anyone who killed or captured the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, or Abu Bakr. Suraqa was sitting with his people when a man walked up: I just saw figures moving along the coast. I think it's them. Suraqa knew it was. And he said out loud: no, that's just some travelers we know. He wanted the reward for himself. Today: Suraqa's horse.
screen: `A PRICE ON TWO HEADS.` → `FIGURES ON THE COAST.` → `NO, JUST SOME TRAVELERS.`

segments.voice: He waits a little, goes home, and quietly sends his horse out behind a hill. He takes his spear and rides. As he nears them, his horse stumbles and throws him. In his own telling, he draws lots with divining arrows, the custom of the time, and the answer comes out against him: don't harm them. He rides anyway, close enough, he says, to hear the Prophet reciting. He notices the Prophet doesn't look back, while Abu Bakr keeps turning around to look. Then the ground gives way. His horse's forelegs sink into the earth up to the knees, and he's thrown. He urges the horse up; it can barely pull its legs out, and when it stands, dust rises from the tracks of its legs like smoke. He draws lots again, and again the answer is the one he doesn't want. At last Suraqa does what a hunter doesn't do. He calls out to the men he's chasing and asks for safety. They stop. He tells them everything: the reward, what people are planning. He offers them food and supplies. They take nothing. They ask only, in effect: keep our matter hidden. He asks for a written promise of safety, and Amir ibn Fuhayra, Abu Bakr's freed man, writes it for him on a piece of leather. The fugitives never run faster. The chaser is the one who's stopped, by the ground and by his own lots, until he gives up the chase himself. The man who set out to sell them ends up guarding their secret, holding their promise in his hand.
screen: `HE RIDES ANYWAY.` · `CLOSE ENOUGH TO HEAR HIM RECITE.` · `THE HORSE SINKS TO THE KNEES.` · `THE HUNTER ASKS FOR SAFETY.` · then, large: `KEEP OUR MATTER HIDDEN.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're chasing right now, a win, an argument, someone's approval, and notice how it feels to keep riding after it. Then picture your horse's legs slowing in soft sand, and instead of fighting it, let it stop, and ask what might happen if you called out instead of charging. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you which chases to let go.
Suraqa's horse. In Bukhari, its legs sink into the ground as Suraqa chases the Prophet for the reward, until he gives up the chase and asks for safety. Today's word.
Your line: the sand held him back. Nobody outran anybody that day. That's day seven hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims retell Suraqa ibn Malik's chase from his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari as part of the hijrah story.

chat.says: How did the Prophet and Abu Bakr get away from Suraqa? Were they just faster?
options: No. His horse sank into the ground until he gave up and asked for safety.
Yes. Their camels outran his horse along the coast road.
They paid him more than the reward, so he turned back home.
chat.meaning: In Suraqa's own account, his horse sank to the knees; he called out for safety, and they asked only that he keep their matter hidden.

Suraqa ibn Malik.meaning: the rider who chased them for the reward

Quraysh.meaning: the tribe that led Mecca and offered the reward

Amir ibn Fuhayra.meaning: Abu Bakr's freed man, who wrote the promise

Abu Bakr.meaning: the Prophet's companion on the road
